comparisons.peer_topic: General business overview and technology focus
comparisons.peer_summary: AMD is a high-performance and adaptive computing leader driving innovation through technology, software, and product leadership to power data centers and AI.
comparisons.comparison: Both NVDA and AMD describe their core business identity as providing high-performance computing solutions for data centers and AI. NVDA defines its Compute & Networking segment to include Data Center accelerated computing platforms and AI software (NVIDIA AI Enterprise). AMD similarly identifies itself as a leader in high-performance and adaptive computing, explicitly stating its technologies power data centers and artificial intelligence (AI). Both companies frame their segment composition or business overview around the critical role of data center and AI workloads.

sentences.text: The Compute & Networking segment is comprised of our Data Center accelerated computing platforms and end-to-end networking platforms including Quantum for InfiniBand and Spectrum for Ethernet; our NVIDIA DRIVE automated-driving platform and automotive development agreements; Jetson robotics and other embedded platforms; NVIDIA AI Enterprise and other software; and DGX Cloud software and services.
AMD is the high performance and adaptive computing leader, powering the products and services that help solve the world's most important challenges.

Our technologies advance the future of data centers, powering the cloud services that have become an essential part of how we work, game, and connect to network, PCs, edge computing, and artificial intelligence (AI).

comparisons.peer_topic: x86 Ecosystem Strategy and Advisory Group
comparisons.peer_summary: Intel's core strategy relies on the x86 ecosystem, advancing it through microarchitectures focused on performance and efficiency. In 2024, the company created an advisory group to expand ecosystem compatibility, simplify software development, and identify future architectural needs.
comparisons.comparison: Both NVDA and Intel describe their product portfolios as spanning from data center to edge and AI applications. NVDA's Compute & Networking segment includes Data Center platforms and extends to edge/automotive (DRIVE) and software services (DGX Cloud). Intel describes its product offerings as providing end-to-end solutions that scale from the data center to network, PCs, edge computing, and AI. Both disclosures highlight a comprehensive architecture approach covering data center compute and adjacent high-growth areas like AI and edge networks.

comparisons.peer_summary: Networking demand in 2024 was driven by AI deployments, DDR5 platform adoption, and increasing data transfer requirements.
comparisons.comparison: Both NVDA and Micron identify AI-driven data center workloads as the primary demand driver for their respective technologies within the data center networking and compute ecosystem. NVDA describes its segment as including accelerated computing and networking platforms (InfiniBand/Ethernet) that support these workloads, while Micron explicitly states that its networking demand in 2024 was driven by AI and DDR5 platform deployments, noting increasing data transfer requirements across industries. Both disclosures highlight the shift toward memory-intensive and high-bandwidth needs in AI-centric data centers.

comparisons.peer_summary: CNBU data center sales were driven by server demand in cloud and enterprise markets, with growth fueled by the shift of infrastructure and workloads to the cloud and the memory-intensive nature of AI data-centric workloads.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures discuss the interplay between cloud infrastructure shifts and AI workloads driving component demand. NVDA includes DGX Cloud and Data Center platforms in its Compute & Networking segment, reflecting the infrastructure side of AI computing. Micron similarly notes that overall cloud growth is driven by the shift of infrastructure and workloads to the cloud, and specifically that cloud servers supporting AI workloads require significantly increasing quantities of DRAM and HBM. This parallels NVDA's inclusion of AI Enterprise software and Data Center platforms, illustrating the complementary hardware and software/memory demands of the same AI infrastructure trend.
